youtube.aciklama:
How can audiology services be delivered remotely? In this lesson we learn about synchronous and asynchronous tele-audiology, the facilitator model, remote testing and fine-tuning, the limits set by calibration and background noise, and the regulation on remote health services in Türkiye. This is not legal advice; check the current legislation.

AIHEAR Audiology Academy makes short, clear lessons for audiology students and professionals.

Sources: Swanepoel DW, Hall JW. A systematic review of telehealth applications in audiology. Telemedicine and e-Health (2010); ASHA, Telepractice (Practice Portal); World Health Organization, World Report on Hearing (2021); Regulation on the Provision of Remote Health Services, Türkiye (Official Gazette, February 10, 2022, No. 31746).

This video is for educational purposes and does not replace diagnosis or treatment.

cumleler: Hello, and welcome to the AIHEAR Audiology Academy.
With this lesson we begin the section on current topics and professional development, starting with tele-audiology.
We will cover synchronous and asynchronous services, remote testing and fitting, the limitations, and the regulations in Türkiye.
Tele-audiology is the remote delivery of audiology services through communication technologies.
It is the audiology branch of what is more broadly called telehealth.
Its main goal is access: reaching people who live far away, have limited mobility, or cannot come to the clinic because of work.
A call from home instead of hours of travel for a short adjustment saves time and money.
In areas with few audiologists, specialist knowledge can reach the patient through a local health worker.
Tele-audiology does not replace in-person care; used with the right patient and for the right purpose, it complements it.
In synchronous service, the audiologist and patient are connected at the same time; a video call or live remote testing are examples.
The audiologist controls the remote computer and test equipment from their own screen and watches the patient on camera.
In asynchronous service, data are first collected and stored, and then reviewed later by the specialist.
For example, video otoscopy images and automated audiograms taken at a screening site can be sent and read the next day.
In a hybrid model, both approaches are used: data are collected in advance, and results are shared with the patient in a live call.
The model is chosen based on the type of service, connection quality and the patient's needs.
In many remote tests, the patient is at a local health center.
There, a trained facilitator places the earphones and probe and assists the patient.
The test equipment is controlled by the remote audiologist over a computer connection.
The audiologist runs the test, monitors responses and interprets the result; the clinical decision is the audiologist's responsibility.
The outcome is a report, recommendations and, if needed, referral for an in-person evaluation.
Facilitator training and a written workflow are the foundation of this model's reliability.
Hearing screening is the most common use of tele-audiology; it can be done at school, at work or in the community.
With a calibrated audiometer and a suitable environment, pure-tone thresholds can be obtained remotely.
Video otoscopy images can be stored and sent, so findings such as earwax or discharge are seen by the specialist.
For tympanometry and otoacoustic emissions, the probe is placed by the local facilitator.
Speech tests are sensitive to sound quality and the connection; the accuracy of the presentation level is checked separately.
The auditory brainstem response, or ABR, can also be controlled remotely, with a local worker placing the electrodes.
Such remote ABR services have been reported especially in some countries with few specialists.
Systematic reviews have shown that, under suitable conditions, remote results can be similar to in-person tests.
The biggest limitation of remote testing is that it cannot always take place in a sound-treated booth.
Booth walls and sound-absorbing material keep background noise below the permitted level.
A test at school or at home has no such guarantee; low-frequency thresholds are especially affected by noise.
So earphones that better attenuate outside noise are used, and background noise is measured during the test.
When the noise limit is exceeded, the result at that frequency is counted as invalid or flagged.
Calibration is also critical: the earphone used must be calibrated together with that device.
A result from an uncalibrated earphone or an ordinary consumer headphone is not a threshold, only an estimate.
Dropped connections or delays can disrupt the timing of sounds and patient responses, so response times are monitored.
Measurements needing bone conduction and masking are harder remotely; vibrator placement depends on the facilitator.
Tests for young children, such as visual reinforcement audiometry, need a two-person team and experience, so they are hard to do remotely.
Because images and health data travel over the internet, a secure system approved by the institution is used.
The patient may lack a device, an internet connection or digital skills, which can create a new inequality in care.
The principle of justice from the ethics lesson applies here too: technology should widen access and leave no one out.
So when choosing remote care, the clinician first asks whether the patient has these resources.
Remote fine-tuning often starts with a patient complaint, for example that their own voice sounds muffled.
Many current hearing aids can connect to the audiologist's software through an app on the patient's phone.
Once connected, the audiologist changes the device settings from their own screen.
The patient hears the change right away in their own environment and gives feedback, an advantage the clinic cannot offer.
Every change, its reason and the patient's reaction are documented.
The initial fitting and verification with real-ear measurement are mostly done in person; remote adjustment complements them.
By reviewing the device's data logging remotely, daily hours of use and common listening environments can be seen.
Questionnaires measuring hearing aid benefit and satisfaction can be completed online before the appointment.
A video call is well suited to counseling new users and training them in communication strategies.
Simple problems with batteries, wax filters or connections can often be solved together on camera.
For cochlear implant users, remote programming is a method that has been studied and is used in some centers.
Auditory training and auditory verbal therapy sessions can also be run with the family by video.
Check-up appointments, small adjustments and counseling are where tele-audiology fits best.
People who live far away, use their device regularly and are comfortable with technology are also good candidates.
Sudden hearing loss, ear discharge or pain, however, need fast, in-person evaluation.
Diagnostic assessment of infants needs a detailed, long test battery, so it is usually done in person.
New-onset dizziness is also referred to the clinic for examination and vestibular testing.
The rule is simple: if a red flag is noticed during a remote session, the patient is called in for an in-person evaluation.

cumleler.yazi: In Türkiye, remote health services are governed by a regulation published in the Official Gazette No. 31746 of February 10, 2022.
cumleler.ses: In Türkiye, remote health services are governed by a regulation published in the Official Gazette number thirty one thousand seven hundred forty six of February tenth, twenty twenty two.

cumleler: The Regulation on the Provision of Remote Health Services covers all health professionals who take part in such services.
It defines remote health care as a service a health professional provides through a remote health information system.
Under Article 8, a health facility that meets the conditions for remote services receives an operating permit from the Ministry.
Under Article 12, a session cannot be recorded on video or audio without the explicit consent of both parties.
Article 14 prohibits forcing a person booking an appointment to receive remote care.
Under Article 9, the patient is told in advance that remote care cannot be equivalent to in-person care.
This is not legal advice; check the current legislation and your facility's permit before planning remote services.

sahneler.metin: Before a remote session, do a short connection test with the patient and tell them which number you will call if the session drops.
cumleler: A tip from the field: do a short connection test with the patient the day before the first remote session.
Use this test to check that the camera, the microphone and the hearing aid app are working.
Tell the patient at the start which number you will call them from if the session drops.
For a patient with hearing loss, captions or a text chat window make a video call much easier.

maddeler.metin: Calibration and background noise are critical

cumleler: Tele-audiology is delivered in synchronous, asynchronous or hybrid models; a local facilitator is key to many remote tests.
The reliability of remote thresholds depends on calibrated earphones, background noise monitoring and connection quality.
Remote fine-tuning and follow-up bring check-ups and counseling into the patient's own environment.
For sudden loss, discharge, pain or new dizziness, the patient is referred for an in-person evaluation.

sahneler.soru: Which is an example of asynchronous service?
secenekler: Later review of stored otoscopy images
sahneler.aciklama: In asynchronous service, data are _stored first_ and reviewed by the specialist later.

cumleler.yazi: Test yourself: which of the following is an example of asynchronous tele-audiology?

cumleler: The correct answer is B: later review of a stored otoscopy image.
In the other options, the audiologist and patient are connected at the same time, so they are synchronous services.
